messages.subject: Multiple Legend Scales in a Single Row
messages.subject_clean: Multiple Legend Scales in a Single Row
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm plotting some data using colour and shape to highlight different aspects. I want my legend to appear horizontally at the top of the plot. Currently the scales appear horizontally at the top, but as two separate rows. Does anyone know how I can tell ggplot to merge both into a single row? Ultimately, I intend to share one legend between two side-by-side plots so there should be enough space across two columns for the legend to be flattened like this.

This snippet illustrates roughly what I've got at the moment.

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(color, clarity, colour = carat, shape = cut)) + geom_point() + opts(title = "Example", legend.position="top", legend.direction = "horizontal")

Thanks,
Alastair

messages.subject: Re: data and manual colours doesn't fit - how to solve it ?
messages.subject_clean: data and manual colours doesn't fit - how to solve it ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Look at

> str(df)
'data.frame':   4 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ CULTURE: Factor w/ 4 levels "BLE TENDRE","MAIS GRAIN",..: 1 2 4 3
 $ TAUX   : num  0.3 0.1 0.4 0.2
 $ COULEUR: Factor w/ 4 levels "#00FF00","#604800",..: 4 1 3 2

Notice that both CULTURE and COULEUR are factors, and observe that
their default levels are lexicographically ordered. You need to order
the levels of one of the two factors to be compatible with the
ordering of the other; one way is to match them using the values =
argument of scale_fill_manual(), but another way is to reorder the
levels of one or both of the factors in the data frame prior to
invoking ggplot().

HTH,
Dennis

http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

Dear all,

A couple of days ago I posted the following at the r-help mail list
and I was redirected to here, so maybe somebody could help me with
this?

don't like that the legend for "Means" and "Observations" includes a
line, though no line is used in the plot for those two (the line for
"Overall Mean" on the other hand is wanted):

library(ggplot2)
ddf <- data.frame(x = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], 5)), y = rnorm(10))
p <- ggplot(ddf, aes(x = x, y = y))
p + geom_point(aes(colour="Observations", shape="Observations")) +
    stat_summary(aes(colour = "Means", shape ="Means"),
                 fun.y = mean, fun.ymin = min, fun.ymax = max,
                 geom = "point") +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(y), linetype = "Overall Mean"),
show_guide = TRUE)

I tried to map the linetype in geom_point (and stat_summary) to NULL
and I tried to set it to "blank" but neither worked.

Is it furthermore possible to combine the two legends? My preferred
plot would have two symbols with different colours and shapes for
"Means" and "Observations" (but no line) and directly below that a
line for "Overall Mean" (that is all the three items in one legend)?
For that I tried to assign the same names to the legends but this did
not work either.

So any help would be highly appreciated.

Thanks a lot,

Thorn

messages.subject: Re: linetype and geom_boxplot
messages.subject_clean: linetype and geom_boxplot
messages.body_plain:
Here is the quick fix:

library(ggplot2)
library(proto)

GeomBoxplot2 <- proto(ggplot2:::GeomBoxplot, {
  objname <- "boxplot2"
  guide_geom <- function(.) "boxplot2"
  draw_legend <- function(., data, ...)  {
    data <- aesdefaults(data, .$default_aes(), list(...))
    gp <- with(data, gpar(col=colour, fill=alpha(fill, alpha),
lwd=size * .pt, lty = linetype))
    gTree(gp = gp, children = gList(
      linesGrob(0.5, c(0.1, 0.25)),
      linesGrob(0.5, c(0.75, 0.9)),
      rectGrob(height=0.5, width=0.75),
      linesGrob(c(0.125, 0.875), 0.5)
    ))
  }
})

geom_boxplot2 <- function (mapping = NULL, data = NULL, stat =
"boxplot", position = "dodge",
                          outlier.colour = "black", outlier.shape =
16, outlier.size = 2,
                          notch = FALSE, notchwidth = .5, ...) {
  GeomBoxplot2$new(mapping = mapping, data = data, stat = stat,
                  position = position, outlier.colour =
outlier.colour, outlier.shape = outlier.shape,
                  outlier.size = outlier.size, notch = notch,
notchwidth = notchwidth, ...)
}

ggplot(mpg, aes(x=manufacturer, y=cty, linetype=factor(year))) + geom_boxplot2()

presentations, but less well suited for a thesis (unless you get the
fonts right in ggplot and save the png in a very high resolution, but
that will hog up memory, i.e. word will become slow/unstable).

Martin

messages.subject: Re: Trajectories of mean values for groups over time
messages.subject_clean: Trajectories of mean values for groups over time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Torvon,
  your post doesn't include a reproducible example which would make it easier to help.

There are several issues. It looks like your Chernobyl error is from the loess fit for geom_smooth which you don't seem to want.
It also sounds like you are missing data. If you don't want a line for those subjects then restrict the dataset before plotting (make a new data.frame).
Not sure you really wanted to jitter but it can be effective for overplotting when sample sizes aren't huge - but if you do it before you call ggplot2 as you did (the function jitter is from base) then you aren't passing the correct x values to stat_summary
For categorical variables like Sex it is easier to define a factor before plotting so that you can set up the labels for the legend.
I hope this example illustrates one approach to doing what you describe.

library(ggplot2)
data(mtcars)
mtcars$Transmission <- factor(mtcars$am,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("automatic", "manual"))

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl, mpg, color = Transmission)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(w = 0.2, h = 0)) +
  stat_summary(geom = "line", fun.y = "mean")
p

-Allan
R version 2.15.1; ggplot2_0.9.1; 64bit Win7

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've got two scales in my plot legend; colour and shape. In the aes I specify the colour first then shape, and when I'm naming the scales and setting up their values etc I specify the colour then shape scales. Why do they appear in the legend the other way round? I've tried reversing the order in the aes declaration and also the order of the scales calls but to no avail. What does ggplot use to determine the order the legend scales will appear in? I've pruned plot code into the following small example (my actual chart shares a legend between a couple of plots hence some of the legend handling is a bit overkill for just one plot).

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

data <- structure(list(instance = structure(c(1L, 5L, 6L, 11L, 1L, 15L,
                                              13L, 2L, 3L, 7L, 16L, 4L, 5L, 16L, 11L, 7L, 9L, 14L, 15L, 3L,

                                                                                      779L, 841L, 809L, 248L, 642L, 491L, 970L, 642L, 418L, 647L, 220L,
                                                                                      446L, 693L, 662L), overlaps = c(0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L,
                                                                                                                      0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L,
                                                                                                                      0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L
                                                                                      ), room.valid = c(324L, 43L, 244L, 321L, 41L, 306L, 15L, 325L,
                                                                                                        50L, 270L, 235L, 305L, 280L, 286L, 232L, 94L, 261L, 313L, 275L,
                                                                                                        225L, 234L, 242L, 244L, 308L, 237L, 313L, 252L, 270L, 308L, 74L,
                                                                                                        334L, 152L, 234L, 334L, 329L, 321L, 234L, 10L, 250L, 73L), final.timeslot = c(0L,
                                                                                                                                                                                      0L, 0L, 0L, 359L, 0L, 648L, 376L, 417L, 125L, 9L, 0L, 0L, 10L,
                                                                                                                                                                                      64L, 180L, 10L, 11L, 21L, 6L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 6L,
                                                                                                                                                                                      0L, 0L, 0L, 382L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 544L, 444L), three.in.a.row = c(424L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                713L, 559L, 246L, 520L, 672L, 614L, 367L, 473L, 608L, 193L, 208L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                208L, 226L, 31L, 35L, 44L, 55L, 344L, 201L, 369L, 213L, 559L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                96L, 382L, 170L, 349L, 352L, 331L, 122L, 255L, 262L, 366L, 255L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                280L, 246L, 646L, 264L, 355L, 436L), single.event = c(54L, 98L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      190L, 92L, 86L, 70L, 96L, 72L, 82L, 78L, 90L, 39L, 45L, 100L,

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      93L, 142L, 144L), delta = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L,

                                                            "nhoods5"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("instance", "event.clashes", "overlaps", "room.valid", "final.timeslot", "three.in.a.row", "single.event", "delta", "nhoods"), row.names = c(NA, -40L), class = "data.frame")

makePlot <- function(data, title = NULL, display.y = TRUE, legend = FALSE){

    plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = value, y = instance))

    plot <- plot + geom_point(aes(shape = nhoods, colour = delta), alpha=I(0.5), position = position_jitter(width=0, height=0.1))
    plot <- plot + scale_colour_brewer(name="A", palette = "Set2", labels=c("Sum","Min Abs.", "Max Abs.","Fraction"))
    plot <- plot + scale_shape_manual(name="B", values = c(15:18,7), guide="legend")

    plot <- plot + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 1)
    plot <- plot + theme_bw()
    if(legend){
        plot <- plot + opts(title = title, legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "horizontal", legend.key = theme_rect(fill = "white"), legend.box = "horizontal", plot.margin = unit(c(0,1,0,0), "lines")) + guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1)), axis.title.x = theme_blank(), axis.title.y = theme_blank())
    } else {
        plot <- plot + opts(title = title, legend.position = "none", plot.margin = unit(c(0,1,0,0), "lines"))
    }
    return(plot)
}

m.data <- melt(data, id.vars = c("instance", "delta", "nhoods"))
hard.plots <- list(makePlot(m.data, display.y=TRUE, legend = TRUE))

tmp <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(hard.plots[[1]]))
leg <- which(sapply(tmp$grobs, function(x) x$name) == "guide-box")
legend <- tmp$grobs[[leg]]

hard.plots[[1]] <- hard.plots[[1]] + opts(legend.position = "none")

args.list <- c(hard.plots, list(left = "Problem Instance"))
grid.arrange(legend, do.call(arrangeGrob, args.list), heights=unit.c(legend$height, unit(1, "npc") - legend$height), ncol = 1, main = NULL)

I am trying to put together a bar graph that includes two plant species and two ant species as categorical variables and d13C as a dependent variable. I have these variables in two locales. So I would like to have two charts that separates them by locale. I have tried this:

d13<-read.table(file="/Users/paolabarriga/Desktop/fake.txt",header=TRUE,sep="\t")

names(d13)

Paola

messages.body_plain:
On 7/5/2012 12:08 PM, Munish Sikka wrote:
> Hi All,
>
> Can someone please help me with this issue? I am still stuck with it.
>
> Warm Regards,
> Munish
>

> On Thu, Jun 28, 2012 at 11:02 AM, Munish Sikka <sikka.munish-Re5J...@public.gmane.org>wrote:
>
>> Hi,
>>
>> please find a smaller data-set and reproducible code attached with the
>> email. There are two data frames,
>> 1) Comprises mean values for 7 different products (variable_name# input_df)
>> 2) Comprises std. dev of 1 particular product (variable_name# sd_input).
>>
>> I wish to assign the same color to std. dev. plot as is assigned to the
>> mean value of that particular product (i.e. "CASA_GFED_Optimized") but its
>> not happening. Please help me with this.

You have a couple of problems here. First, the geom_smooth call is using
vectors in the aes call, not references to columns in a data.frame
(sd_input in this case would be the appropriate data.frame. This is
partly why there is no association with model (and thus color, etc.). So
the call should look something like (but see later comments for more
changes):

geom_smooth(data=sd_input, aes(ymin=-sd, ymax=sd, colour=model))

Second, when using multiple data.frames, it helps to have any factors
have the same set of levels. Thus I've added a line:

sd_input$model <- factor(sd_input$model, levels=levels(input_df$model))

which gives the model variable in sd_input the same levels (in the same
order) as in your main dataset (input_df).

Third, since you are doing any specific smoothing (you've already
summarized your data), you might as well use geom_ribbon which can help
get around some other problems (no specification of y/flux in sd_input,
e.g.). An appropriate alpha must be specified, though.

Fourth, since model is already a factor, you don't need to wrap
references to it in factor(); in fact it may cause problems since not
every data.frame has every level present.

Fifth, since the data.frame for geom_ribbon (sd_input) doesn't have flux
(the variable mapped to the y aesthetic), just put that in the geom_line
and not the general call.

Putting this all together, and stripping out everything unneeded from
your example, re-writing the code that created your initial data.frames
(using dput on the results of what you had), and re-ordering the
building of chart into a single statement gives:

library("ggplot2")

plotName <- 'Comparison of latitudinal averages'
xlims <- c(65,80) # x axis extent

input_df <-
structure(list(flux = c(0.08733913, 0.1015934, 0.1244135, 0.1390303,
0.08417182, 0.02371609, -0.404555985, -0.274926953, -0.267656303,
-0.319995352, -0.345494975, -0.312800453, 6.8e-06, -3.08e-05,
-0.00052447, -0.001651782, -0.008117757, -0.012909356, -7.4e-06,
0.000350601, -0.007354754, -0.014550594, -0.034726184, -0.061246906,
-0.000439617, -9.11e-05, -0.001032338, -0.003649731, -0.017603566,
-0.038499236, -0.000440385, -0.000154135, -0.002382317, -0.013099981,
-0.036534534, -0.0651667, -0.000134273, -0.000257972, -0.000677862,
-0.0006657, -0.000582543, -0.000784166), model = structure(c(5L,
5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L,
3L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 7L, 7L, 7L, 7L, 7L, 7L), .Label = c("ACOS",
"CASA_GFED_Optimized",
"CLM4CN", "EC_MOD", "MPI_BGC", "OCN", "VEGAS"), class = "factor"),
     lat = c(79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69, 79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69, 79,
     77, 75, 73, 71, 69, 79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69, 79, 77, 75, 73,
     71, 69, 79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69, 79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69)), .Names =
c("flux",
"model", "lat"), row.names = c(NA, -42L), class = "data.frame")

sd_input <-
structure(list(sd = c(0.962702227, 0.922861425, 0.916777851,
1.023710254, 1.177481079, 1.041598737), model = structure(c(1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = "CASA_GFED_Optimized", class = "factor"),
     lat = c(79, 77, 75, 73, 71, 69)), .Names = c("sd", "model",
"lat"), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

sd_input$model <- factor(sd_input$model, levels=levels(input_df$model))

chart <- ggplot(input_df, aes(x=lat, group=model, colour=model,
fill=model)) +
     geom_ribbon(data = sd_input, aes(ymin = -sd, ymax=sd), alpha=0.5) +
     geom_line(aes(y=flux), size=1.0) +
     opts(title=plotName,legend.position='bottom') +
     scale_x_continuous('Latitude',limits=xlims) +
     scale_y_continuous(expression(paste('Latitudinal average of NEE
', (g~C~m^{-2}/day)))) +
     scale_colour_discrete(name='Model') +
     scale_fill_discrete(name='Model')
print(chart)

>> Another query is to assign multiple columns to the legend in the bottom of
>> the graph.

The scale functions can do this.  Say you want it to be in 2 rows, then
you add guide=guide_legend(nrow=2) to the scales call; ncol can also be
specified if you prefer. I would also recommend supressing the legend
elements created by the ribbon since they don't really help that much.
That is done by adding a show_guide=FALSE to the geom_ribbon call.
Together, this is:

ggplot(input_df, aes(x=lat, group=model, colour=model, fill=model)) +
     geom_ribbon(data = sd_input, aes(ymin = -sd, ymax=sd), alpha=0.5,
show_guide=FALSE) +
     geom_line(aes(y=flux), size=1.0) +
     opts(title=plotName,legend.position='bottom') +
     scale_x_continuous('Latitude',limits=xlims) +
     scale_y_continuous(expression(paste('Latitudinal average of NEE
', (g~C~m^{-2}/day)))) +
     scale_colour_discrete(name='Model', guide=guide_legend(nrow=2)) +
     scale_fill_discrete(name='Model')

ggally_points <- function(data, mapping, ...){
  p <- ggplot(data = data, mapping = mapping) + geom_point(...)
  p$type <- "continuous"
  p$subType <- "points"
  p
}

library(GGally)

         myt = myt,
         x1 = sin(myt),
         x2 = sin(myt+0.05),
         x3 = sin(myt+pi/8),

         x4 =  cos(myt))

ggally_path <- function(data, mapping, ...){
  p <- ggplot(data = data, mapping = mapping) + geom_path(...)
  p$type <- "continuous"
  p$subType <- "path"
  p
}

Hi,

You can use the directlabels package for this:

car <- read.csv("demo.csv")

library(ggplot2)
#install.packages("directlabels")
library(directlabels)

car$Var <- abbreviate(car$variable)

p <- ggplot(data=car,
            aes(x=X.10.130, y=value, colour=Var)) +
  geom_line()

direct.label(p+xlim(min(car$X.10.130), max(car$X.10.130)+30))

Best,
Ista

On Sat, Jul 7, 2012 at 7:09 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Brandon:
>
> Joran is on the right track, and in fact you can find a suitable template example on the ggplot2-0.9 help pages. I needed some practice, so came up with this:
>
> require(MASS)

>
> require(ggplot2)
> require(scales)
> df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(15000),y=rnorm(15000))
>

> # 2D density estimate using MASS::kde2d with
> # conversion to data frame:
> dens <- with(df, kde2d(x, y), n = 50, lims = c(-4, 4, -4, 4))
> ddf <- data.frame(expand.grid(xd = dens$x, yd = dens$y),
>                   z = as.vector(dens$z))
>
> p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
>       geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
>       stat_contour(data = ddf,
>                    aes(x = xd, y = yd, z = z, color = ..level..),
>                    size = 1)
> p + scale_color_gradient(low = 'maroon', high = 'yellow',
>                          guide = 'colorbar')
>
> or alternatively,
>
> ggplot() +
>   stat_contour(data = ddf, geom = 'polygon',
>                aes(x = xd, y = yd, z = z, fill = ..level..)) +
>   geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y),
>                size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +

messages.subject: Re: Ordering Scale Legends
messages.subject_clean: Ordering Scale Legends
messages.body_plain:
For the future reference of any interested parties who encounter this problem I posted a more concise of this question on StackOverflow. The author of the guides functionality, Kohske Takahashi, kindly posted an answer <http://stackoverflow.com/a/11397958/844418>. To summarise his response, essentially the ordering in version 0.9.1 (or less) is unpredictable. He's fixed this in the upcoming 0.9.2 release, and you'll be able to control the order of a legend key by passing an explicit order parameter to the guide_legend function.

messages.subject: Re: geom_tile with gradientn
messages.subject_clean: geom_tile with gradientn
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't know if this is precisely what you wanted, but here's one
approach using the cut() function (findInterval() is another option):

fm$clr <- cut(fm$z, breaks = c(-1, -0.5, -0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 1))
cols <- c('yellow', 'orange', 'black', 'red', 'green')

ggplot(fm, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = clr)) +
    scale_fill_manual('sin(x + y)', values = cols) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

cut() has a labels = argument that you can use to replace the default
half-open intervals, and you may well want a different set of breaks
than what I've used above, but this should give you the basic idea.
I've also expanded the x and y scales so that the graph covers the
entire plotting region, in case that's of interest.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
> Note that the value 0 certainly does not map to black.
> I tried using values=brks  in the gradientn, but that made it even worse.
> Any suggestions?

If you want to map specific values to specific colours, you need a
couple of additional pieces, as shown in the examples in
scale_fill_gradientn:

cols <- c('yellow', 'orange', 'red', 'black', 'green')
brks <- c(-1, -0.5, -0.25, 0, 1)
( ggplot( fm)
   + geom_tile( aes( x=x, y=y, fill=z))
   + scale_fill_gradientn(
     name = 'sin(x+y)',
     limits = c(-1, 1),

     colours = cols, breaks=brks, labels=brks , values= brks,
     rescaler = function(x, ...) x, oob = identity
))

Hadley

		p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = mod,

               	show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames =
TRUE,
               	show.rownames = TRUE,
               	gpar.rowtext = gpar(col = "black", cex = 1.0, fontface
= "bold")))

When changes started to fly on ggplot2 and then ggExtra was
deprecated, there were some e-mails and suggestions about how to do a
table annotation in the new system.  But, so much more has changed
since then.  Can you guru's give me a suggestion about where to look
to begin restoring this functionality?  Unless of course it is already
in there and I can't find it.  This would be a single table in a
single panel; no faceting.

Thanks so much for not only this answer but all the work that's gone
into ggplot2 and friends lately.  Bryan

messages.subject: Re: My code for Tuftian scatterplots with quartile plots as axes
messages.subject_clean: My code for Tuftian scatterplots with quartile plots as axes
messages.body_plain:
Since the quartile axes are added using grobs, the reference names "axis-l-3-3" and "axis-b-4-4" in the gPath function would most likely have to be adjusted. Unfortunately I haven't worked with grobs enough to know for sure. As of right now they're hardcoded but there is probably a clean way to have the code iterate through the different facets and edit the standard axis grobs to be quartile ones.

After looking at this thread: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5380417/is-there-a-way-of-manipulating-ggplot-scale-breaks-and-labels where breaks are generated per-facet, it may not be necessary to create a separate data frame containing the breaks but instead specify breaks=function(data)as.numeric(quantile(data))

Best of luck,
Mikhail

> Ben

messages.subject: repost: is new layer possible in ggplot similar to as.layer of latticeExtra
messages.subject_clean: repost: is new layer possible in ggplot similar to as.layer of latticeExtra
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Is it possible to implement the idea of as.layer() of latticeExtra in ggplot2?

In simple terms it the function looks like

as.layer(x, x.same = TRUE, y.same = TRUE,….)

where  x is a trellis object/drawing.

For example if I have two plots x1 and x2, I can print x1 and use as.layer to superimpose/overlay x2 over x1 and have the option of specifying x.same=TRUE /FALSE and y.same = TRUE/FALSE. This is probably similar to what par(new = T) in base graphics.

This will help in

a) get a quick visual idea on relation between two variables of different scales (not undermining the facets use, but cannot simply cannot ignore the advantage and insight that one gets of having able to draw variables on the same plot)

b) having a dual axis in ggplot. First overlay (using as.layer) and display labels on right y axis as described  by Kohske in thread https://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/ff73e6f891280aa1/079d7bff5b803799?lnk=gst&q=semantic+differential#079d7bff5b803799

Thanks and Regards,

S.N.V. Krishna

>

First overlay (using as.layer) and display labels on right y axis as described  by Kohske in threadhttps://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/ff73e6f891280aa1/079d7bff5b803799?lnk=gst&q=semantic+differential#079d7bff5b803799 <http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/ff73e6f891280aa1/079d7bff5b803799?lnk=gst&q=semantic+differential#079d7bff5b803799>

There are pretty strong feelings regarding having several variables with different scales on the same plot. The argument could be summed up to this I think: the first thing your eye is drawn to in a line plot with dual axis (which is the most common use) is the points where the lines intersect; these points are completely artificial and depend only on the scales chosen on the y axes; instead of giving you insights on the data such a plot diverts your attention away from the data, and worse, give you "false" information.

Therefore, dual axis graphics are bad™.

While I don't disagree with the reasoning, I am not a particular zealot of the cause. I am merely point out the issues that were previously mentioned on this list.

On 2012-Jul-11, at 22:31 , keith p. kolley wrote:
>
> allan - the original data doesn't go below zero but the smoothed data does.  i figured out how to demonstrate the problem more clearly than my original attempts:
>
>> library(ggplot2)
>> y<-rep(0:1,each=20,times=5)+runif(10,0,0.05)
>> x<-seq(1:length(y))
>> ggplot()+geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_smooth(aes(x=x,y=y),method='loess',span=0.20,se=F)
>
> the bottom of the smoothed data dips below y=0 even though the sampled data does not. i wanted to cap the smoothed line to stay above y=0.

You can discard the points (even smoothed ones) below 0 with scale_y_continuous() or just zoom in to not see them with coord_cartesian()

library(ggplot2)
y<-rep(0:1,each=20,times=5)+runif(10,0,0.05)
x<-seq(1:length(y))

ggplot()+geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_smooth(aes(x=x,y=y),method='loess',span=0.20,se=F) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0, 1.2))
ggplot()+geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_smooth(aes(x=x,y=y),method='loess',span=0.20,se=F) + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 1.2))

Previously, one was able to supply NA or Inf to one of the limits (instead of 1.2 here) and it ggplot would then use the default computed. This does not seem possible anymore so you have to hard-code a value here, which is not always desirable.

If you want to line to actually become flat at zero, then you need to compute your loess smoother before ggplot and then use geom_path

On 2012-Jul-12, at 19:06 , Navi wrote:
>
> I want to discretize the variables or plot them as continuous.
> So i suppose i need to do something with Scale_colour_discrete or Scale_colour_discrete to either plot large continuous variables as continuous, so that R can split it into reasonable categories and plot the smaller values as factors.

You have to do the splitting outside of ggplot, with cut() and then ggplot will detect that these are factors and do the appropriate thing with them.

It won't be possible though to have part of the scale discrete and the rest continuous (you mention "plot the smaller values as factors" suggesting that you want the highest ones to be continuous)

> In addition it missed out the lower and upper limits of the values in the scales. So i need to figure out a way to display all those values.

Actually, while you only see a few squares of color, all values in your data set a mapped to different colors. The squares are just there to show you the colour corresponding to a few round numbers (you would not want 82.3452 to be displayed on your scale do you?). Add:
	scale_fill_continuous(guide="colorbar")
and you'll see: the colours on the plot do not change but the legend makes it more explicit that it is a continuous scale.

> However, i am not able to figure out how to assign the limits and colour schemes to my variables values.

limits cf above (otherwise with the limits argument)

to change the colours and use something other than blue use
	scale_fill_continuous(low="red", high="yellow")
for example. If you want more than two colours, look at the functions I mentioned in my previous email.

I think this topic was discussed long back, most probably in the
R-help. That time also Hadley quite clearly mentioned that he was not
going to implement it in ggplot system! I also feel that having a plot
with two different y-axis is not a good idea from scientific plotting
view-point as it looks like having two suns in the sky (such system
cant support any meaningful life-system due to the huge variation in
the temperature)!!!

In case, the underlying two variables are in different units therefore
their ranges are different significantly, then I think the best idea
is to plot them in Logarithmic scale or use some transformation to
make them unit free. In the case of the transformation there will not
be any loss of information as you are dividing/multiplying all values
by same constant (I prefer respective starting values therefore you
can make both of them to start from the same number like 100 and then
see their progress over time). This also makes sense from the point
that, plotting these 2 variables in the same canvas means you are
actually comparing their movements over time (assuming they are time
series data).

HTH,

Thanks and regards,

messages.body_plain:
My guess is that the problem has something to to with the function to
check for zero range from the scales package:

library("scales")
zero_range(c(-1e-13,1e-13))

To check for equality to zero, zero_range() uses the function
all.equal(), which has a default tolerance of .Machine$double.eps^0.5.
 The y-axis limits from your example are much smaller than that.

So I don't know if there is a quick fix.  Maybe patching the scales
package with a different zero_range() function could solve the
problem.

- Andreas

messages.subject: Re: creating a bar plot after using model.tables(fit,"means")
messages.subject_clean: creating a bar plot after using model.tables(fit,"means")
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Rule 1 in using ggplot2 is that the input is (almost) always a data
frame [there are a few exceptions if you use qplot(), but ggplot()
requires a data frame]. Therefore, if you want to take output from
model.tables() and plot it in ggplot2, you have to do a little bit of
data surgery. Here's a reproducible example.

DF <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(1:3, each = 10)),
                  y = rnorm(30))
m1 <- aov(y ~ gp, data = DF)
u <- model.tables(m1, type = 'mean', se = TRUE)
str(u)

m1summ <- data.frame(gp = as.numeric(levels(DF$gp)),
                     mns = as.vector(u$tables$gp),
                     se = as.numeric(u$se) )

# An error bar plot with a line connecting the group means:
ggplot(m1summ, aes(x = gp, y = mns)) +
    geom_line(size = 1, colour = 'orange') +
    geom_point(size = 3, colour = 'blue') +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mns - se, ymax = mns + se),
                    width = 0.3, size = 1)

I believe a bar chart is not a good way to plot the group means. The
above plot doesn't exactly enthrall me, either, but it's a distinct
improvement from a bar chart.

BTW, the help files for version 0.9.0 are located at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/docs/. The site that Jean-Olivier mentioned
is for version 0.8.9.

HTH,
Dennis

Hi

I notice a strange behaviour when using geom bar with 2 observations per x-axis unit. Dodge won't work in general with this, unless the two observations per unit are "identified" by a fill/colour. But if this fill/colour does not create a clear cut groups1/group 2 for each unit, then one has a mixed case of stack/dodge.

Maybe I am doing something wrong, should not use for example the stat identity?

library(ggplot2)

messages.body_plain:
The devtools package allows you to maintain the CRAN version of a
package and the development version of the same package as separate
entities. The trick is to install development versions under dev_mode,
so that the development version is available when dev_mode is ON and
not available when dev_mode is OFF. You can tell when dev_mode is ON
because the prompt changes to d>. Packages installed under dev_mode
are kept in a separate library (see below) so that they don't clash
with the CRAN versions.

If you install the development version of a package when dev_mode is
OFF, it overwrites the CRAN version. In general, that's a bad idea,
but for an actively developed package like ggplot2, it's an especially
bad idea.

Suggestion:
(1) Reinstall the CRAN version of ggplot2 (and any other package that
you may have inadvertently overwritten with a development version).
(2) Do the following to install and use development versions of
packages (I deliberately put in the prompts so that you can see what
is done when dev_mode is ON and what is done when dev_mode is OFF):

> library('devtools')
> dev_mode()
# install the development versions of packages
# when dev_mode is ON
d> install_github('ggplot2')
d> install_github('scales')
d> install_github('gtable')
# load the installed development versions
d> library(ggplot2)
d> library(gtable)
d> packageVersion('ggplot2')   # should be 0.9.2
   <...do whatever else you like..>
d> dev_mode()    # turn off dev_mode
> library('ggplot2')
> packageVersion('ggplot2')  # should be 0.9.1 if current

If you open the HTML help pages when in dev_mode, you'll find an extra
set of help pages corresponding to the development versions of
packages you've installed under dev_mode in a separate library. If
you're not in dev_mode, those pages will not appear because the
packages are not available (or visible, if you will) outside of
dev_mode because the location of that library is not in .libPaths.
Using my Windows system as an example, you can see this as follows:

## dev_mode ON
d> .libPaths()
[1] "C:/Users/Dennis/R-dev"               "C:/Users/Dennis/R/win-library/2.15"
[3] "C:/Program Files/R/R-2.15.1/library"
d> dev_mode()
Dev mode: OFF
> .libPaths()
[1] "C:/Users/Dennis/R/win-library/2.15"  "C:/Program Files/R/R-2.15.1/library"

HTH,
Dennis

Sent: 19 July 2012 13:06

Cc: ggplot2 (ggp...@googlegroups.com)
Subject: Re: gtable_height function not found

The devtools package allows you to maintain the CRAN version of a package and the development version of the same package as separate entities. The trick is to install development versions under dev_mode, so that the development version is available when dev_mode is ON and not available when dev_mode is OFF. You can tell when dev_mode is ON because the prompt changes to d>. Packages installed under dev_mode are kept in a separate library (see below) so that they don't clash with the CRAN versions.

If you install the development version of a package when dev_mode is OFF, it overwrites the CRAN version. In general, that's a bad idea, but for an actively developed package like ggplot2, it's an especially bad idea.

Suggestion:
(1) Reinstall the CRAN version of ggplot2 (and any other package that you may have inadvertently overwritten with a development version).
(2) Do the following to install and use development versions of packages (I deliberately put in the prompts so that you can see what is done when dev_mode is ON and what is done when dev_mode is OFF):

> library('devtools')
> dev_mode()
# install the development versions of packages # when dev_mode is ON
d> install_github('ggplot2')
d> install_github('scales')
d> install_github('gtable')
# load the installed development versions
d> library(ggplot2)
d> library(gtable)
d> packageVersion('ggplot2')   # should be 0.9.2
   <...do whatever else you like..>
d> dev_mode()    # turn off dev_mode
> library('ggplot2')
> packageVersion('ggplot2')  # should be 0.9.1 if current

If you open the HTML help pages when in dev_mode, you'll find an extra set of help pages corresponding to the development versions of packages you've installed under dev_mode in a separate library. If you're not in dev_mode, those pages will not appear because the packages are not available (or visible, if you will) outside of dev_mode because the location of that library is not in .libPaths.
Using my Windows system as an example, you can see this as follows:

## dev_mode ON
d> .libPaths()
[1] "C:/Users/Dennis/R-dev"               "C:/Users/Dennis/R/win-library/2.15"
[3] "C:/Program Files/R/R-2.15.1/library"
d> dev_mode()
Dev mode: OFF
> .libPaths()
[1] "C:/Users/Dennis/R/win-library/2.15"  "C:/Program Files/R/R-2.15.1/library"

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: ggplot: plot x position values on graph with y values
messages.subject_clean: ggplot: plot x position values on graph with y values
messages.body_plain:
I'd melt the data:

here's one approach. there's probably a less arbitrary way than this when it comes to dodging the pos label from the variable label

#first, melt the data
df.melt <- melt (df,id.var=pos)

#plot same data with two different labels
ggplot(df.melt,aes(pos,variable))+
geom_text(aes(label=variable))+
geom_text(data=subset(df.melt,value>0.1),aes(x=pos+.1,y=variable,label=value))

Adam Loveland

From: DavidE <davidroh...@gmail.com>
To: ggp...@googlegroups.com
Date: 07/20/2012 02:46 PM
Subject: ggplot: plot x position values on graph with y values
Sent by: ggp...@googlegroups.com

ggplot2 users:

A plotting question. I have a data frame consisting of one column of 317 x position values (pos), and 20 columns of y data values (A,C,D,.....), arranged like this:

pos  A    C    D  ...
1     0.1 0.2 0.01
2     0.4 0.1 0.001
3     0.0 0.05 0.001
.
.
.

I am using ggplot () + geom_text(data=df, aes(pos, A, label="A", colour="red")) to plot out the letter A based on its value. I would also like to plot the pos number next to A if the value of A is >0.1 (to plot A2, for instance). I can manage to do this using the generic plot function using this code:

plot (1:317, df$A[1:10], pch="A", cex=1,col="A")
for (j in 1:nrow(df)) {
       if (df$A[j] >= 0.1) {
           text(j, df$A[j], j,pos=4, offset=0.2,  col="black", cex=0.7)
       }
}

I'm having trouble using the same strategy with ggplot2. I can think of adding additional columns to the data frame to call when plotting - like this:

pos  A    A1
1     0.1  NA
2     0.4   2
3     0.0   NA
.
.
This solution seems rather clunky. Is there an equivalent strategy for ggplot2?

Thanks for your suggestions.

--

messages.body_plain:
It's not a bug. You're using stat_identity, which means you are telling ggplot to not do anything at all to your counts. Since you have multiple rows for the secondary category, ggplot faithfully reproduces this in the plot, with multiple segments for each row. I believe what you really want to do is to finish aggregating the counts by type outside of ggplot (using ddply or something similar) and the plot using that completely aggregated data set.

messages.body_plain:
If you look at the code in the ggplot2 package, you'll see the
following. At present, ggplot2 is in the third position on the search
path on my system, which explains the function call:

> objects(pos = 3, pat = 'scale_colour')
 [1] "scale_colour_brewer"     "scale_colour_continuous"
 [3] "scale_colour_discrete"   "scale_colour_gradient"
 [5] "scale_colour_gradient2"  "scale_colour_gradientn"
 [7] "scale_colour_grey"       "scale_colour_hue"
 [9] "scale_colour_identity"   "scale_colour_manual"

In other words, there are ten (exported) scale_colour* functions, but
none of them are scale_colour() per se - the help page you cited uses
scale_colour as an abbreviation for any or all of the above functions.

Dennis

messages.subject: Generating straight lines to connect points on a plot with coord_trans(y="log10")
messages.subject_clean: Generating straight lines to connect points on a plot with coord_trans(y="log10")
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have an x-y scatter plot for which I want to compute summary statistics by group (mean and SEM) on the original data and then plot on a log scale. coord_trans(y="log10") does exactly the right thing, including showing the error bars as asymmetric on on the transformed plot.

I'd like to connect the points with straight lines to "guide the eye" but can't figure out how to do this without having them curve. I tried geom_line and geom_path but neither seemed to do the right thing. I can get the lines to be straight by replacing coord_trans(y="log10") with scale_y_log10(breaks=breaks) but then the summary statistics are computed on the log10 transformed data.

Is there a way around this? Thanks in advance for any help!  Here is a toy example:

library("ggplot2")

errorLowerSEM <- function(x){
        x.mean <- mean(x,na.rm=TRUE)
        x.sd <http://x.sd> <- sd(x,na.rm=TRUE)
        SEM <- x.sd <http://x.sd> / (sqrt(length(x)))
        return(x.mean - SEM)
}

errorUpperSEM <- function(x){
        x.mean <- mean(x,na.rm=TRUE)
        x.sd <http://x.sd> <- sd(x,na.rm=TRUE)
        SEM <- x.sd <http://x.sd> / (sqrt(length(x)))
        return(x.mean + SEM)
}

cat <- c(rep("A",6),rep("B",6),rep("C",6))

messages.subject: Re: Correlation values in each cell of facet grid
messages.subject_clean: Correlation values in each cell of facet grid
messages.body_plain:
You could do something like this:

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point()

# Calculate correlation for each group
cors <- ddply(mtcars, c("vs", "am"), summarise, cor = round(cor(mpg, wt), 2))

p + facet_grid(vs ~ am) +
  geom_text(data=cors, aes(label=paste("r=", cor, sep="")), x=30, y=4)

I don't think it's possible to make this come out correctly with margins=TRUE, though. If you want the margins, you may need to preprocess your data to add an ALL value for each faceting variable.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: change label of margin from "(all)" to "Total"
messages.subject_clean: change label of margin from "(all)" to "Total"
messages.body_plain:
On 7/24/2012 11:11 AM, Anvar Suyundikov wrote:
> How do I change the label of margin grid from "(all)" to "Total" ?
>
> mg <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(cyl)) +  geom_point(stat="bin", size = 2,
> aes(shape = gear, position = "stack"))
> mg + facet_grid(carb ~ gear, margins = TRUE)
>
> Thanks

Since the "(all)" group is created inside the ggplot code, there is not
a direct mechanism to do it. However, by utilizing the labeller argument
to facet_grid, you can change the labels however you want, including
replacing one of them.

label_renamemargin_gen <- function(newname="Total") {
   function(variable, value) {
     value <- as.character(value)
     value[value == "(all)"] <- newname
     value
   }
}

mg + facet_grid(carb ~ gear, margins = TRUE,
                 labeller=label_renamemargin_gen("Total"))

Details on how labeller (and labeller generators) work is on the wiki:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/labeller

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

Hi:

Question: Since bar charts are anchored at zero (on a frequency scale)
by definition, what is log(0)? Consequently, why would you want to
supply a logarithmic scale to a bar chart? Perhaps a frequency polygon
would be more appropriate if you want to express frequency on a
logarithmic scale (assuming, of course, that all of the class
frequencies are >= 1); see geom_freqpoly().

messages.subject: Re: Logarithmic y-axis scale with barchart
messages.subject_clean: Logarithmic y-axis scale with barchart
messages.body_plain:
My response was to the suggestion of using log(freq + 1/6) to scale
frequencies. Since bar charts are anchored at y = 0, it is considered
a Bad Idea to use a logarithmic scale to represent frequencies. The
issue has been debated on this list several times and I don't intend
to rehash it. IMO, using log(x + 1/6) or whatever is a cosmetic fix to
the problem, but if anyone wants to implement such a scale, they're
welcome to do so. The tools are in the scales package.

I suggested geom_freqpoly() because it doesn't require a geometric
object that is anchored at zero, but it has the same scaling problems
if a category has zero frequency. OTOH, if you have large frequencies
in every category, the vertical axis won't have to contain zero
frequency, unlike a bar chart.

In reply to a similar email from me, Hadley told me that he actually always viewed points  as being all outline. Seen that way, the choice makes sense. But it doesn't work already, so it's not as though someone can use odd
combinations of shapes and set fill with one parameter.

# changes the outline color for 0 and 23 and the fill color for 19; 23
is hollow even though it can take a fill value
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(gear), y=mpg, shape=factor(gear),
colour=factor(gear))) + geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values=c(0,
19, 23))

# sets 23 fill value and leaves 0 and 23 outline black, and 19 fill black
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(gear), y=mpg, shape=factor(gear),
fill=factor(gear))) + geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values=c(0,
19, 23))

# sets 0's outline and fill/outline for 19 and 23
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=factor(gear), y=mpg, shape=factor(gear),
colour=factor(gear), fill=factor(gear))) + geom_point() +
scale_shape_manual(values=c(0, 19, 23))

Regarding the first part of your email, that makes sense. I didn't
realize ggplot2 was just accessing settings already in existence. I
suppose I have to change my point to be that R strikes me as a bit
schizophrenic. All shapes would seem to have a bg= value whereas only
21 and up have an outline (whether that be called via col= or stroke=
or something similar).

Since it's hard coded in R, I don't see a good way around this...

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Jul 26, 2012 at 4:05 PM, Jean-Olivier Irisson
<iri...@normalesup.org> wrote:
> On 2012-Jul-26, at 22:38 , John Hendy wrote:
>>
>> Sure. But my point still stands. If colour maps to outline and fill
>> maps to inner fill and some points have *no* outline... I'd expect it
>> to be set via fill, not colour. In other words, if there's only a
>> fill, it's set with colour=. If there's a fill and an outline, fill is
>> set with fill and outline is set with colour. That doesn't make sense
>> to me.
>
> In reply to a similar email from me, Hadley told me that he actually always viewed points  as being all outline. Seen that way, the choice makes sense. I think the confusion comes from the default shape in ggplot with indeed seems to be only a fill, but most shapes (the 15 first actually) are only and outline. It would be a pain to have to change between fill and colour when you change shapes.

Yeah, put that way, I guess it does make sense. Since I hardly use the
shapes and mostly just pass color options, I was only thinking of pch
19 and missing the fact that the others take a col value for outline,
not fill (or bg).

>
> My personal opinion is that there should be fill and stroke and that colour would be a "smart" aesthetic that changed either fill or stroke depending on the shape/geom (stroke for some points shapes, fill for others, stroke for path, fill for polygon etc.). But it's probably too late for that ;)

This makes sense. Per baptiste above, though, since ggplot has to send
things via the built in R pch grammar... it does get tricky to have
"smart" aesthetics when col= works for outline and bg for < 21 and
col= is the outline and fill= is the fill for > 21. It actually seems
up the user to pass things correctly... or perhaps to simply pick
either > 21 or < 21 for all pch styles. This simplifies things. In
fact, that's what I did for my own example. Instead of just replacing
geom_bar() with geom_point() + coord_flip(), I used geom_bar(pch=21)
so I wouldn't have to change my fill= setting :)

John

messages.subject: Shape palettes?
messages.subject_clean: Shape palettes?
messages.body_plain:
The recent discussion of the lack of standardization for colors and
fills had me thinking about ways that specifying symbol shapes could be
improved by having pre-set palettes, similar to how color brewer works.

Typically, mapping shapes to a factor can lead to very unsatisfactory
choices, as you may end up with a mish-mash of symbols, some solid,
others hollow, and otherwise. It would be nice if there were predefined
palettes that you could specify via scale_shape.

One example I would find useful would be a "paired" shape palette, which
could repeat shapes when using the "paired" color palette from color brewer.

Do others think this would be helpful? Am I overlooking some easy way to
accomplish this, other than specifying the values you want for each
symbol? Does ggplot already have a "smart" way to deal with shape palettes?

Thanks!

--

messages.subject: Re: cannot make unique verticale lines on each facet of density plot/hitogram
messages.subject_clean: cannot make unique verticale lines on each facet of density plot/hitogram
messages.body_plain:
The simplest way to do this is to create a small data frame that
contains the x-intercepts as one variable and the grouping factor
being used to create the facets as the other. When you call
geom_vline, you use that data frame as the input data. The safest
thing to do is to make the name of the x-variable of this data frame
the same as the one in the original data frame fed to ggplot2 and
ditto with the grouping variable name. Here's a simple example:

DF <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(1000), x2 = rnorm(1000, 2, 0.5),
                 x3 = rnorm(1000, -1, 1.5))
library('ggplot2')
library('reshape2')
DFm <- melt(DF)

DFlines <- data.frame(value = c(0, 2, -1), variable = paste0('x', 1:3))

ggplot(DFm, aes(x = value, colour = variable)) + geom_density() +
   facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 1) +
   geom_vline(data = DFlines, aes(xintercept = value))

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Axis tick marks for scale_x_discrete
messages.subject_clean: Axis tick marks for scale_x_discrete
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't think you can do that in ggplot2. Axis ticks are controlled by
the theme_segment() function in the current theming system, whose
arguments are colour, size and linetype. What you're asking for would
require positional adjustment arguments such as vjust and hjust, which
do not exist in theme_segment() or theme_line(). You can offset the
axis tick _labels_ (which can be modified with theme_text()), but not
the axis ticks per se AFAIK.

My guess is that in order to get what you want, some surgery using the
grid package may well be necessary.

Dennis

2012/7/16 Jean-Olivier Irisson <iri...@normalesup.org>

> Forgot to reply to the list.
>
> On 2012-Jul-16, at 11:11 , Jean-Olivier Irisson wrote:
> > On 2012-Jul-15, at 17:09 , Manuel Spínola wrote:
> >>
> >> Is there any simple example on how to work with the new geom, "geom_map", with a shapefile to make a choropleth?
> >
> > You need to read the shapefile into a data.frame and then use geom_map on this data.frame. Ideally, we should have a fortify() function that takes the shapefile and converts it into a data.frame for you but that's not the case yet.
> >
> > Here is example code for a points shapefile. It does the have the pretension to be universal but it might help you start:
> >
> > library("shapefiles")
> > library("plyr")
> >
> >    # read files
> >    shape = read.shapefile(name)
> >
> >    # get shapes
> >    X <- shape$shp[[1]]
> >    nbShapes <- length(X)
> >
> >    # prepare storage for the coordinates
> >    d <- data.frame()
> >
> >    # for each shape in the shapefile
> >    for (i in 1:nbShapes) {
> >        # select the shape
> >        x <- X[[i]]
> >
> >        if (length(x$parts) > 1) {
> >            # If there are several parts in this shape
> >            # separate parts from the next one with NA
> >            pointsL <- split(x$points, cut(1:nrow(x$points), breaks=x$parts))
> >            pointsL <- llply(pointsL, rbind, NA)
> >            # store everything back in a data.frame
> >            points <- do.call(rbind, pointsL)
> >        } else {
> >            points <- x$points
> >        }
> >
> >        # suppose that the coordinates are lon and lat
> >        names(points) <- c("lon","lat")
> >
> >        # create an identifier for each shape, if necessary
> >        if (nbShapes > 1) {
> >            points$id <- i
> >        }
> >        # and add NA to separate this shape from the next shape
> >        points <- rbind(points, NA)
> >
> >        # store everything in the data.frame
> >        d <- rbind(d, points)
> >    }
> >
> >    # remove the NA at the last position
> >    d <- d[-nrow(d),]
> >
> >    # add information from the dbf
> >    if (!is.null(d$id)) {
> >        d[,names(shape$dbf$dbf)] <- shape$dbf$dbf[d$id,]
> >    }
> >
> >

On Tue, Jul 31, 2012 at 3:43 PM, Jean-Olivier Irisson
<iri...@normalesup.org> wrote:
> On 2012-Jul-31, at 22:37 , Giovanni Azua <brav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>

>
> It's because the text is repeated as many times as there are lines in your data frame. Try putting the data=df in the geoms that need it and not in the gloabl ggplot() call. If that does not work, you'll want to create a custom data.frame with just the required data.
>
> But overall, I think this text does not look like data, more like a custom annotation. So for this you should prefer annotate() with geom="text". You would expect the horizontal lines to be the same (i.e. annotate with geom="hline") but for some reason I never managed to get this working...

Jean-Olivier is right - you want something like:
  annotate(geom="text", x=5, y=5, label="text label")

In general when you want to add a single geom, you can use annotate()
and specify the geom.

The only exception is that annotate() doesn't work with hline, vline,
and abline. There is some long-standing code (probably from before
annotate() existed) in those geoms that handles the special case where
the intercept is set to a specific value. When you do that, it will
only plot one line, instead of one for each row in the data frame.
Unfortunately, this code also makes it not work properly with
annotate().

There's a patch waiting to be merged that will change the behavior to
be like other geoms. The new behavior can break existing user code, so
it's waiting for the next major release to be merged.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It's nice that you provided us with the code, but without a
corresponding dataset (preferably small) that throws the error, there
isn't much one can do to help you. Since this is a common oversight on
this list and on R-help, I decided to use this as an opportunity to
explain how to properly send data to the list (i.e., it isn't just
you! :)

If data confidentiality is a problem, then create a fake data set with
different names but the same overall structure. One way to do this is
to provide code that generates the (possibly fake) data; another is to
apply the dput() function to your R data object and send its output in
the e-mail. For example,

# generate fake data with code:
set.seed(457)  # makes the random data reproducible
DF <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = LETTERS[1:5], z = rnorm(5))

# Output the structure of the data object DF
dput(DF)

#### this is the part you would copy and paste into an e-mail:
structure(list(x = 1:5, y = structure(1:5, .Label = c("A", "B",
"C", "D", "E"), class = "factor"), z = c(-1.00645455517947, -1.54059755758232,
1.29604764063258, -0.505431013487536, -1.04079687811305)), .Names = c("x",
"y", "z"), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")
####

If you copy and paste this into your R session and assign it to an
object named DF, you should be able to exactly reproduce this:
> str(DF)
'data.frame':   5 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ x: int  1 2 3 4 5
 $ y: Factor w/ 5 levels "A","B","C","D",..: 1 2 3 4 5
 $ z: num  -1.006 -1.541 1.296 -0.505 -1.041

OTOH, if I had just copied and pasted this instead:
> DF
  x y         z
1 1 A -1.006455
2 2 B -1.540598
3 3 C  1.296048
4 4 D -0.505431
5 5 E -1.040797

how are you supposed to know if x is integer or numeric, or that A is
factor or character? These apparently small differences can matter
when trying to diagnose problems. So either use direct code or dput()
to avoid potential sources of confusion.

The advantages of dput() on an R data object include:
(i) the output is in text form, which makes it easy to send in an e-mail;
(ii) the structure of the data object is preserved, which means that
    someone who copies and pastes it into her R session from your
e-mail can be assured
    that its contents are exactly the same as in your R session. Copying
    and pasting data from a text editor, a web site or an R session
cannot provide
    the same guarantee.

Hopefully you're not the only one who might benefit from this advice :)

Dennis
